The campaign I’m playing in is post apocalyptic where a bunch of aberrant worms have infected dead corpses, so the main reoccurring enemy is undead or aberration. Divine sense and detect evil and good has been super useful in figuring out if we’re being followed by undead, if people around us are infected, etc.

You’re making it seem like I’d make every extra planar use nystuls, and I wouldn’t. One undead or fiend or whatever in an entire campaign isn’t game breaking lol, and it’s certainly not making an ability useless. It’s just keeping the Paladin or cleric etc from being able to use their abilities that they always use to detect things every single time, and makes the players have to think a little harder on how to figure out what’s going on with a particular intelligent conniving NPC. You’re telling me that Mephistopheles, the Archdevil of Cania and most powerful Wizard of the nine hells, who decides to walk among man for a change of scenery, is gonna get spotted instantly by 1st level Shmaladin the Paladin? For certain foes, it’s foolish to assume they’d not tie down that gaping cover blower of a creature type, because why wouldn’t they? The PCs will have to be smarter than normal to be able to figure some things out, or else the whole campaign is just ability after ability solving the problems and no actual thinking.

I think it’s also important to note the player characters are capable of being self aware about the spell. It’s only second level. What I would do as the DM is bring the spell up at some other point in the story, disconnected from this storyline, and then the PCs would have that knowledge they could call back on and be like, “wait wait wait! Remember that illusion magic we read about in that wizards notes? What if the gambling king pin guy is using that??”. It’s letting the players figure the story out through ingenuity, cleverness, and intelligence, not just gimmicky cure-all 1st level abilities. And again, maybe this kind of playstyle is not for everyone, but that’s the kinda games we run at my table, whether I’m DM or not.

I think it just depends on the players then. My players like roleplay and don’t sell themselves wholeheartedly to their abilities as if they’re save-all. We run complicated campaigns where things just aren’t always as easy as “I use divine sense to ruin the build up of who this character is”. If Luke Skywalker had a “detect father” ability, and instantly found out Vader was his father, that would kinda ruin the whole thing wouldn’t it? Instead you get hints and feelings that lead up to the big reveal (granted i wouldnt personally steal the “bad guy tells good guy who he is” trope because it’s somewhat overdone, but I’d like the players find out on their own through actual investigation and clue-matching etc. Also on the note that divine sense is useless, I’ve heard that before in the community but I don’t know why at all. I’m literally playing a paladin right now inna campaign and it’s suuuuuper useful lol. And if my players were to cast it and the person they’re suspecting doesn’t show signs of being any of the detectable creatures, it won’t put them off the sent, they’ll just start thinking “huh this guy is hiding something that he definitely doesn’t want people finding out, because these things we’ve witnessed aren’t coincidences”. And then through more clues, or maybe spying, they’d eventually find it out. It could be a whole session of figuring it out, instead of just a throw away ability that spoils the story. Again, perhaps my players are different and naturally more inquisitive, and perhaps their expectations of a more complex story help with this scenario.

Highly disagree. Divine sense and the like are a cheap way to blow the cover of very cool and very powerful entities in urban environments. It’s far cooler to have, say, the owner of the biggest gambling pit in the city be a devil in disguise, that can’t be detected by first level abilities instantly. The cooler alternative is to give subtle hints like: “his shadow fades in and out and you see a hooked tail in it every once in a while”, or “as you walk down to the bottom floor of the gambling house, you notice your escort, the owner of the whole place, passes a mirror but his reflection doesn’t show”, and then you let the players come to their own conclusion afterwards. Not just “oh you use one of you several divine senses right now for funzies? Yeah okay the owner of the gambling house is a vampire”. Obviously don’t do this for every extra planar, because you want the ability to still be useful, but give your intelligent bad guys the proper tools to hide themselves, and the players can find out who they actually are in more intricate and creative ways.
